splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations in criminal or quasi-criminal contexts. The Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity, while the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits hold that lenity prevails. This affects how ambiguous sentencing enhancements and criminal provisions are construed.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity must be applied before deferring to an agency's or the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of an ambiguous criminal or sentencing provision, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference (under Auer/Kisor/Stinson) takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's commentary to control the interpretation of ambiguous sentencing guidelines even when the result is anti-defendant.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the guideline text, which does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can expand the text of the career-offender guideline to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy when the guideline text itself is silent on the matter. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others hold the text is unambiguous and excludes inchoate offenses. This affects thousands of career-offender designations under the federal sentencing guidelines.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses included
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a valid interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes under Stinson deference.

positions.label: Guideline text is unambiguous — inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses from the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' and the commentary impermissibly expands the guideline's scope.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether a defendant must satisfy all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is disqualifying. The Ninth and Eleventh Circuits read 'and' conjunctively, while the Fifth, Sixth, Seventh, and Eighth Circuits read it disjunctively. This affects mandatory minimum sentencing for thousands of federal drug defendants.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) when the state criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal controlled substances schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the sentencing guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the underlying substance to be federally scheduled. Some circuits hold that any state drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling, while others require the substance to be on the federal schedules. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: State offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Substance must be federally scheduled
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Henderson as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) validly authorizes such consideration.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits hold that non-retroactive statutory changes cannot contribute to such a finding, while other circuits have been more permissive. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) purported to allow it, but the Seventh Circuit held that provision exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot, alone or in combination with other factors, constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and the Sentencing Commission lacks authority to say otherwise.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider non-retroactive changes in sentencing law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, particularly when combined with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may also use civil rights actions such as Bivens.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging conditions of confinement that affect their liberty interests (such as BOP decisions on earned time credits or transfer to prerelease custody), or whether civil rights claims provide an alternative path. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged this unresolved conflict that has persisted for over half a century, affecting how prisoners challenge BOP decisions under the First Step Act and other statutes.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is available (and may be exclusive) for challenges to conditions of confinement that implicate the fact or duration of imprisonment, such as BOP decisions on earned time credits.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions (§ 1983 or Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement even when habeas corpus might also be available, so long as the challenge is not to the fact or duration of confinement itself.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Spencer v. Haynes discussion

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs after a Chapter 13 petition is filed but before conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit holds that such appreciation inures to the estate, while other circuits have held the opposite. This split affects debtors who convert in good faith and has significant implications for the treatment of homeowners' equity in bankruptcy.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a) compel the conclusion that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure, policies, and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to the debtors who converted in good faith, not to the estate.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Castleman dissent as contrary authority

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order in a criminal case is governed by the civil deadline (30 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)) or the criminal deadline (14 days under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b)).
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but acknowledged a lopsided circuit split on the issue.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Onamuti as minority position

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the violation of supervised release conditions at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be oriented toward reentry and rehabilitation purposes.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release, placing it at odds with other circuits that hold supervised release revocation should be focused on the defendant's breach of trust and reentry needs rather than retribution. This split affects how revocation sentences are calculated and justified for hundreds of individuals facing supervised release revocation each year.

positions.label: Courts may punish for supervised release violations
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose punishment for violations of supervised release at revocation hearings, permitting a punitive purpose in revocation sentencing.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Lewis / United States v. Esteras

positions.label: Revocation should focus on reentry, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to address the defendant's breach of the court's trust and facilitate reentry, not to impose additional punishment for the underlying violation.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Esteras dissents as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing for selecting actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability under ERISA's multiemployer pension provisions. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay. The split implicates whether plans must finalize assumptions before year-end or may update them afterward.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in withdrawal liability calculations.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in SCOTUS cert petition as opposing view

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about the limits of judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to retain jurisdiction to revoke supervised release even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as stated in the judgment regardless of the supervisee's flight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the gatekeeping provision of § 2244(b)(1), which bars successive habeas petitions raising claims that were previously presented, applies to federal prisoners proceeding under § 2255. If it applies, federal prisoners face a categorical bar on raising any previously presented claim, in addition to § 2255(h)'s own requirements. This affects the ability of federal prisoners to obtain collateral review of their convictions.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the successive-petition bar of § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, categorically barring them from re-raising any previously presented claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own requirements for successive motions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to challenge election rules before an election takes place. The split affects whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures can proceed or must wait until after the election, with significant implications for mail-in voting rules and ballot counting deadlines nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election laws that may affect the counting of votes, based on competitive injury theory.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election laws before an election because they have not suffered a concrete, particularized injury in fact.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in SCOTUS cert description (Bost v. Illinois)

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the denial of a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment. Other circuits have taken varying approaches to the appealability of sealing order denials, creating uncertainty about when privacy-based sealing orders are immediately appealable.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that the denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost if review were delayed until final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because the category of claims can be adequately vindicated through post-judgment appeal or other means.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits disagreed on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, including issues of liability and available remedies. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach, indicating a potential circuit split on the applicable legal framework for fair treatment in hospitality, retail, and service industries.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that business operators face broader liability for discrimination claims, with more expansive remedies available to aggrieved customers.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards apply to discrimination claims against business operators, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
